title: Is Anything Exposed When It's All Laid Bare?; Both Hamlet And Hitchcock Find

contact_edits.before: They're less firmly rooted than in Whistle, because the text gives them less help. As in the film, you're left wondering what it's all for. Are we only here to see, yet again, the bourgeoisie exposed, the elders rotten, the youngers maimed? Probably yes. These characters don't just have skeletons in their closets; they're skeletons themselves. But they certainly rattle with style. Eric Peterson's Helge is more tetchy than tyrannical, if he carried more weight, the play might. Rosemary Dunsmore, though, is superb as his wife, alternately soothing and goading her offspring in a set speech dripping with poisoned politesse. (It's the high point of the play as it was of the film.) Allan Hawco and Philip Riccio, the company's founders, again play brothers, Hawco weak and vicious (last time he was strong and vicious), Riccio an ambiguous avenger. Caroline Cave is rather wasted as Michael's wife, who gives near as good as she gets but has to give most of it early. Tara Rosling transforms herself as Helene; as her nerves go, she seems more and more like a Nordic Janice Soprano. And so it goes, down a fine line that includes Earl Pastko's implacable maitre d' and Nicholas Campbell's understandably depressed tycoon. The entire cast is on red alert. This is about as close as we'll get to pure theatre, with all the limitations that implies and all the excitement. - Festen runs until Dec. 13 at the Berkeley Street Theatre. For ticket information, call 416-368-3110.
